title: Ghosthunting at one of America's most haunted places: Why it's a bad idea
excerpt: Ghosthunting at one of America’s most haunted places: Why it’s a bad idea
content:
The first thing I noticed upon stepping foot outside was a sudden burn and itch on my right inner wrist. A new scratch mark had appeared out of nowhere — that’s how I knew I shouldn’t have gotten myself into this ghosthunting trip. If you’re looking to stay safe and not mess with any bad spiritual energy or whatever supernatural forces may be out there, I advise you to stay away too. 

I write this opinion piece as a warning to anybody who’s genuinely thinking of going ghost hunting. My friends and I went to Lake Shawnee, an abandoned amusement park that’s supposedly one of the most haunted places in America. We willingly paid to stay the night, a decision I was second-guessing as soon as it got dark. 

Before I delve into the dangers of ghost hunting, I do want to preface with the importance of supporting a place like Lake Shawnee. As it’s a historical site, paying to stay the night and learning about the property actually helps them fund to preserve the area. The property is owned by a man named Chris White, who has familial connections tied to the land. He said there isn’t anything bad-natured residing within the property, but we experienced otherwise. 

Ghost hunting, spirit searching or any activity centered around the idea of actively seeking out the paranormal automatically invites the potential for bad experiences to happen. What explains these experiences isn’t always clear-cut, but as a skeptic myself, there are things I genuinely cannot explain that happened that night. I’m writing this article the morning after, sleepily typing on my phone in the passenger seat with weird incidents to blame for lack of sleep. 

The scratch on my arm is the first piece of evidence as to why this was such a bad idea. As soon as I first stepped out of the vehicle onto the land, I felt a sudden yet minor burning and itching sensation on my arm. I looked down, and a fresh scratch was imprinted onto my inner wrist. It felt like a normal scratch, yet more noticeable than I had typically experienced. This may be hypervigilance to blame, but there was nothing that could’ve possibly scratched me. I took a photo of the mark on my phone, and about an hour later, it was completely gone.

At this abandoned amusement park is a rusted swing set that’s supposedly haunted by a little girl who was killed there. When my group of friends approached this swing set, there was a crowd of people surrounded around two of the swings, which were swaying back and forth while the other 30 swings remained completely still. It was almost as if two people were gently swinging back and forth. I caught a video of it — the sight was truly eerie. 

Later that night, my friends and I retreated back into one of our cars to get out of the cold and warm up a little. One of the old, battered-up paddle boats out on the lake that was initially across the body of water had suddenly drifted to our side, pointed at us. No one had prompted the raft to move, which makes me question what it was doing near us. The entire afternoon it had resided on the opposite side of the lake, stationed by the Fallout inspired “Paddle Boats” sign. It was, quite frankly, like someone was watching us. It almost felt like a paranormal-adjacent male gaze. 

Around 1 a.m., we explored the property a little more then went to bed, sleeping haphazardly in any space we could muster inside our cars. I was suddenly awoken by my friend in the middle of the night with a gesture toward the window. There were now multiple handprints visible on the windows, which had become covered with a thin layer of condensation from our breathing. I went back to bed, trying not to think about who had left that there.

In the morning, we were awoken by my friend from the other car panicking. I opened the door to the vehicle I was sleeping in, where she quickly showed me her leg. There was a clear red imprint of a large hand that appeared to have grabbed around her calf. We waited tensely while she called her mother, clearly freaked out. Writing this a few hours later, the red mark is still there, and we’re not how long it’ll remain. She’s tried rubbing it off to no avail, thinking maybe it was some kind of stain. I was thankful to have documented this as evidence. 

I wasn’t the only one who felt like something strange had occurred. “There was definitely something there. What was it? No idea. But there was definitely something there.” Konrad Landess said the morning after, when we stopped at a restaurant called Tudor’s Biscuit World in the outskirts of Princeston, W. Va. The surrounding town had an interesting energy to it, and the restaurant we went to felt like a time warp — like we were “in the end scene of a horror movie,” as another friend put it. 

I’m not saying to completely avoid ghosthunting if you can, but I am saying to tread carefully and know what risks you’re getting into. As a skeptic myself, I cannot attest to whether what my friends and I experienced that night was actually caused by the paranormal. But what I can say is that what happened absolutely happened. And, in the end, it might be better to stay out of trouble instead of going looking for it.
